topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Custom memory management is justified by a workload contract, not by the belief that ordinary allocation is inherently unacceptable. A monotonic arena can serve a bounded phase and release storage together; a pool can reuse a fixed number of object slots. This chapter builds both with explicit exhaustion and lifetime rules, including generation-tagged handles that reject a stale reference after a slot is reused.

blocks.text: A request-processing service allocates thousands of short-lived objects, then discards them together. A phase-based arena may fit that lifetime pattern. Another service repeatedly reuses a fixed number of slots, but clients retain identifiers after release. A generation-checked pool may fit that identity problem. These are different requirements, even though both are often described as “custom memory management.”

blocks.text: This chapter starts with the workload and lifetime model before choosing an allocator. The examples deliberately use standard facilities where possible: a PMR monotonic resource for bounded phase storage and ordinary optional objects for a small slot pool. The goal is to make exhaustion and reuse explicit without introducing unnecessary raw-storage hazards.

topics.title: 10.1.2 Understanding Allocation Overhead
topics.summary: Allocation can involve bookkeeping, synchronization, alignment, cache effects, and calls into a broader memory manager. The cost varies by size, contention, lifetime pattern, and implementation. Measure the actual path before replacing it with a specialized allocator that introduces new restrictions.

blocks.text: A custom policy often trades flexibility for predictability: fixed capacity, phase-based lifetime, no individual reclamation, or limited object types. Document those restrictions as part of the API. Counting fewer calls is useful evidence, but it does not alone prove lower end-to-end latency or lower total memory use.

blocks.text: Allocation overhead includes more than the cost of obtaining a pointer. It can involve metadata, synchronization, size-class selection, page management, and cache effects. The workload also pays for construction, initialization, destruction, and any data movement caused by container growth. Measuring only the allocator call can miss the dominant cost of the complete operation.

blocks.text: A monotonic arena often makes individual deallocation cheap because storage is reclaimed as a phase. That does not make every workload cheaper. If long-lived and short-lived objects share one arena, the long-lived objects can delay reclamation of a large amount of otherwise-dead storage. The lifetime grouping must match the application’s phases, not merely the convenience of passing one resource pointer everywhere.

blocks.text: Container growth can consume multiple arena blocks over a phase. Destroying an old buffer may not recover its space for reuse within a monotonic resource. Reserving a known upper bound can therefore change peak arena demand substantially. However, reserving an unrealistic maximum for every request can waste more space than controlled growth. Compare the actual allocation history under representative input distributions.

blocks.text: A useful cost model includes peak live storage, peak retained storage, number of upstream requests, and latency distribution for allocation-heavy operations. These measures answer different questions. A pool can reduce average allocation work while still suffering occasional expensive initialization or contention. A real-time claim needs a timing argument that covers those paths, not simply a benchmark with a lower mean.

blocks.text: Do not let a faster allocator hide an unbounded queue or missing resource limit. If the application accepts work indefinitely, improving allocation speed may only accelerate memory exhaustion. The allocator is one layer in a resource policy that also includes admission, capacity, ownership, and reclamation. Later chapters connect those layers through bounded queues and explicit request deadlines. Here, the first engineering decision is whether the workload truly has a phase or slot structure that justifies specialized management.

topics.title: 10.2.1 Implementing Memory Arenas
topics.summary: A monotonic arena allocates successive regions from backing storage and normally reclaims them together. Individual deallocation requests do not return each region for immediate reuse under the basic policy. This fits a phase where many objects share a lifetime boundary, such as parsing one bounded document or constructing one frame’s temporary data.

Individual object destruction does not necessarily make earlier arena space available for subsequent requests. This behavior is useful when a complete request or batch has a clear end.

topics.title: 10.2.2 Implementing Object Pools
topics.summary: An object pool manages a bounded set of reusable slots. It must track which objects are alive, construct and destroy them correctly, and reject allocation when no slot is available. A slot index alone can become stale after release and reuse, causing an old handle to refer to a different object.

blocks.text: Pairing an index with a generation counter lets the pool distinguish successive occupants. Access succeeds only when the slot is live and its generation matches. Counter wraparound needs a policy; this example retires a slot before generation reuse rather than silently accepting an ancient handle. Pool capacity and stale-handle errors remain explicit outcomes.

blocks.text: An object pool reuses a collection of slots. Reuse creates an identity problem: slot three can hold one object now and a different object later. A bare index identifies a location, not a lifetime instance. If a client retains the old index, it can accidentally act on the replacement object. A generation value distinguishes successive uses of the same slot.

reading.title: 10.2.2 Implementing Object Pools
paragraphs: An object pool manages a bounded set of reusable slots. It must track which objects are alive, construct and destroy them correctly, and reject allocation when no slot is available. A slot index alone can become stale after release and reuse, causing an old handle to refer to a different object.

Pairing an index with a generation counter lets the pool distinguish successive occupants. Access succeeds only when the slot is live and its generation matches. Counter wraparound needs a policy; this example retires a slot before generation reuse rather than silently accepting an ancient handle. Pool capacity and stale-handle errors remain explicit outcomes.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Reuse without a lifetime protocol
topics.summary: A request resets its arena while a queued response still contains a view into that storage. The response may appear correct until the next request overwrites the same bytes. The repair is to keep the arena alive through response consumption or copy the required result into an independent owner before release. Resetting later by a guessed delay is not a lifetime protocol.
